newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: NATO fails to keep pace with history - Russia PM.
newsitem.headline: NATO fails to keep pace with history - Russia PM.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday criticised NATO enlargement plans, saying the alliance had failed to keep pace with history.

Chernomyrdin, on the first day of a three-day visit to the Slovak capital, met his Slovak counterpart Vladimir Meciar and President Michal Kovac, talking mostly of further economic cooperation between the two nations with Meciar.

But Kovac's spokesman Vladimir Stefko told Reuters that in talks with the President, the Russian Prime Minister criticised the alliance for not accepting the situation in Europe after the fall of communism.
"Mr Chernomyrdin repeated Russia's categorical opposition to NATO expansion, saying this is not the way to solve the defence situation in Europe," Stefko told Reuters.
Chernomyrdin made no comments on the matter after meeting Meciar, saying he would answer journalists' questions on Tuesday.
Stefko added that Chernomyrdin said that in his view NATO had not been reformed enough since the fall of communism as it was still "too much strategically oriented to the East".
Kovac said Slovakia's desire to join NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) remained a top international policy priority, Stefko said.

"President Kovac told him (Chernomyrdin) the ambition of Slovakia remains to join NATO and no way aims against any political or economic relations with Russia," Stefko said, adding Kovac does not see NATO as being aimed at Russia or its people.
Chernomyrdin arrived in Slovakia early on Monday for talks focusing mainly on developing economic ties, but also covering security and defence issues.
Russia has demanded that NATO should not station nuclear and other weapons in new member states and wants a binding treaty on relations between Russia and the alliance.

Slovakia has said it wants to be among the first group of new members to join the alliance, but its chances appear to have waned after repeated U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of its democratic reforms.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are seen as the countries most likely to be invited to join the alliance, probably at a NATO summit in Madrid in July.
Chernmomyrdin and Meciar finalised a long-term gas delivery contract with Slovakia, which depends on the Russians for virtually all of its natural gas supplies.
The Russian Prime Minister added the two sides further discussed whittling down Russia's $1.5 billion debt to Slovakia which it inherited from the former Soviet Union.
Russia is partly paying off its debt with deliveries of Russian passenger aircraft for Slovakia's nascent civil airline and technology for the Soviet-designed Mochovce nuclear power plant.
"We would, however, also welcome more quality Slovak goods on our market and we are doing all we can to encourage this," Chernomyrdin said.

Chernomyrdin is expected to sign some 12 accords here, covering subjects such as liberalisation of trade, cooperation between the two central banks and the setting up of a committee for cooperation in science and technology.
